title: Open a workbook and read cells
summary: openpyxl opens an .xlsx file as a workbook. A workbook holds sheets, and a sheet holds cells you reach by their address, like ws["B2"], or by row and column numbers.
objectives: Pick a sheet by its name and list the sheet names.
Read a cell’s value by address (ws["B2"]) and by number (ws.cell(row=2, column=2)).
Find how many rows and columns a sheet uses.

slides.h: By the end: read a workbook without opening Excel
slides.say: Meera runs the office at Sharma Traders, a stationery wholesaler in Pune. Every evening she opens stock.xlsx to check a few numbers. By the end of this lesson, three lines of Python read them for her.
points: **openpyxl** is a Python library that reads and writes .xlsx files.
You don’t need Excel installed: Python reads the file itself.
Everything you know from Excel (sheets, cells, A1 addresses) is still there.
p: Meera runs the office at Sharma Traders, a stationery wholesaler in Pune. Every evening she opens stock.xlsx to check a few numbers. By the end of this lesson, three lines of Python read them for her.
**openpyxl** is a Python library that reads and writes .xlsx files.
You don’t need Excel installed: Python reads the file itself.
Everything you know from Excel (sheets, cells, A1 addresses) is still there.

visual.text:
import openpyxl
wb = openpyxl.load_workbook("stock.xlsx")
ws = wb["Stock"]
print(ws["A2"].value, ws["B2"].value)

real.text: runs the office of a stationery wholesaler in Pune and lives in Excel all day.

slides.say: Three layers, as in Excel. `load_workbook` gives the **workbook**. `wb["Stock"]` gives one **sheet**. `ws["B2"]` gives one **cell**, and `.value` is what’s in it.
points: `wb.sheetnames` lists the sheet names, in tab order.
`wb.active` is the sheet that was open when the file was saved.
Forget `.value` and you print the cell object, not what’s in it.

slides.h: The cell, not what’s in it
slides.say: A cell is an object with an address, a value and a style. Printing the cell itself shows its address, which is rarely what you want.
p: A cell is an object with an address, a value and a style. Printing the cell itself shows its address, which is rarely what you want.

lecture.title: Finding your way round a sheet

slides.say: Inside a loop you’ll want numbers, not letters. `ws.cell(row=3, column=2)` is the same cell as `ws["B3"]`: column 1 is A, 2 is B, and so on.
points: Rows and columns both start at **1**, as in Excel (not 0, as in Python lists).
p: Inside a loop you’ll want numbers, not letters. `ws.cell(row=3, column=2)` is the same cell as `ws["B3"]`: column 1 is A, 2 is B, and so on.
Rows and columns both start at **1**, as in Excel (not 0, as in Python lists).

slides.say: `ws.max_row` is the last row that has anything in it, and `ws.max_column` the last column. With a header in row 1, the data is rows 2 to max_row.
points: 7 rows with a header means 6 items.
p: `ws.max_row` is the last row that has anything in it, and `ws.max_column` the last column. With a header in row 1, the data is rows 2 to max_row.
7 rows with a header means 6 items.

visual.text:
import openpyxl
wb = openpyxl.load_workbook("stock.xlsx")
ws = wb["Stock"]
print("Rows:", ws.max_row)
print("Columns:", ws.max_column)
print("Items:", ws.max_row - 1)

points: `openpyxl.load_workbook("file.xlsx")` opens a workbook; `wb.sheetnames` lists its sheets.
`ws = wb["Name"]` picks a sheet; `ws["B2"].value` or `ws.cell(row=2, column=2).value` reads a cell.
Rows and columns start at 1, as in Excel.
`ws.max_row` and `ws.max_column` say how much of the sheet is used.
